title: Pauri 19, meaning: through letters
hookLine: countless names and places; yet through letters we speak the Name and sing His praise (Japji 19)

cards: A child's name in giant wobbly letters, taped to a bedroom door. A small thing doing a big job. A few shapes of ink, and someone across the room, or across the world, or long after, can hear what was meant.
Pauri 19 has just said even countless is too small a word for creation. You'd expect it to give up on words entirely. It doesn't.
It turns and praises the smallest thing we have: the letter.

teach.b: Today's word is akhar: a letter, a written character. Here's the heart of the stanza in the original: akharee naam akharee saalaah. Through letters, the Name.
Through letters, praise. Then, in paraphrase: through letters, knowledge and songs and the singing of virtues. Through letters, writing and speaking.

teach.h: THE WRITER HAS NO FOREHEAD LINES.
teach.b: Through letters, even what's written on each person's forehead, their destiny, is told. Everything we can say about the sacred comes through these little shapes and sounds.
Then a turn: the One who wrote all this has nothing written on His own forehead.

teach.h: SMALL, AND YET THE WAY IN.
teach.b: No one assigns the Writer a destiny. As He commands, so things are received. As much as He has made, so much is His Name.
And without the Name, there is no place at all. So the stanza holds two things together. Words can never contain it.

And yet words are how we reach toward it. That has a place in Sikh life. Sikh tradition credits the second Guru, Guru Angad, with shaping the Gurmukhi script, the letters the Guru Granth Sahib is written in.
Learning those letters is a first step toward reading Gurbani.

One more layer some readers point out: akhar is related to the Sanskrit akshara, a letter or a syllable, a word that can also mean imperishable. The letter that can't hold everything is also a thing that lasts.
That closes the countless stanzas: countless devotions, countless fools, countless names.

how: Pauri 19 is recited in the morning Japji Sahib; learning the Gurmukhi letters, the painti akhar, is a first step toward reading Gurbani.

o: a hymn sung in praise of God
a line written on the forehead

games.q: what's inside Pauri 19 — tap the pairs.

s: Pauri 19 gives up on words because they're too small
it praises letters: through them come the Name, praise and song.
Pauri 19 says the Writer has nothing written on His own forehead
no one assigns the Writer a destiny.
Sikh tradition credits Guru Angad with shaping the Gurmukhi script
the letters the Guru Granth Sahib is written in.

games.q: words can never contain the countless. so what does Pauri 19 say about letters?
o: through letters, we speak the Name and sing praise.
games.why: akharee naam akharee saalaah: through letters, the Name; through letters, praise. small, and yet the way in.

practice: If you have paper or a phone nearby, write one word you love, a name, a place, a quality like kindness or home, slowly, one letter at a time; if you can't write right now, trace it with a finger on your knee.
Look at the shapes and notice how much those few marks carry. Then sit with it, breathing.

wordCard.voice: Akhar. A letter. Through letters, Pauri 19 says, come the Name, praise, knowledge and song; related to the Sanskrit akshara, which can also mean imperishable.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: akhar, a letter; Japji has the form akharee, through letters. From Sanskrit akshara.

carryVoice: Your line: through letters, the name. Small shapes, and yet the way in. Day one hundred ninety-two, done.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 4 (Japji, Pauri 19, the rest of the stanza and refrain)
